article.headline: Ancient Wisdom or Modern Invention? The Emerald Tablets Examined
article.lede: A widely shared image quotes *The Emerald Tablets of Thoth*, presenting its archaic verse as timeless esoteric law: thoughts create reality, emotions shape unseen worlds, cause and effect govern fate. The passage lands in a tradition of Hermetic philosophy — but the text behind it has a more complicated provenance than its antique styling suggests.
article.body:
The quote belongs to *The Emerald Tablets of Thoth the Atlantean*, a text that circulates heavily in New Age and spiritual communities as recovered ancient wisdom. Its actual origins are considerably more recent. The text was authored in the 1930s by Maurice Doreal (born Claude Doggins), founder of the Brotherhood of the White Temple, a Colorado-based esoteric order. Doreal claimed to have physically retrieved the tablets from the Great Pyramid and to be channeling Thoth, a legendary Atlantean priest-king. The archaic register — "know ye," "O man," "ye create" — is a deliberate stylistic choice meant to evoke antiquity.

This matters because *The Emerald Tablets of Thoth the Atlantean* is frequently confused with a genuinely ancient text: the *Tabula Smaragdina*, or **Emerald Tablet** (singular). The Tabula Smaragdina is a short Hermetic fragment — the source of the famous phrase "as above, so below" — preserved in Arabic manuscripts from roughly the eighth or ninth century CE, with roots in late-antique Greek Hermeticism. The two texts share thematic DNA but are distinct works separated by over a millennium of verified history from Doreal's composition.

The ideas in the quoted passage are not without intellectual lineage. The claim that **thought is a creative force** echoes Hermetic and Neoplatonic philosophy, which held that mind or *nous* is the generative principle behind material reality. The insistence on mastering emotion as a precondition for shaping one's circumstances appears in Stoic ethics, in the *Kybalion* (another early-twentieth-century Hermetic synthesis), and in the broader New Thought movement that shaped American popular spirituality from the 1890s onward. Doreal's text recombines these currents into a single dramatic voice.

Whether one reads the passage as genuine mystical transmission or as a creative work in a long tradition of spiritual writing, the ideas it advances — that attention, intention, and self-regulation have causal power over outcomes — are neither new nor inherently fringe. They recur across Stoicism, Vedanta, and modern cognitive-behavioral frameworks, each disciplined tradition arriving at a version of the same claim by different routes. The Doreal tablets dress the argument in cosmic drama; the substance underneath is older than any single text.

concepts.definition: A philosophical and spiritual tradition rooted in texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary synthesis of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth. It holds that mind and spirit are primary — that the inner world shapes the outer — and is condensed in the maxim 'as above, so below.' Hermetic ideas fed into Renaissance alchemy, Freemasonry, and twentieth-century New Age spirituality.

A short Hermetic text preserved in Arabic manuscripts from around the eighth or ninth century CE, later translated into Latin in the medieval period. It is the origin of 'as above, so below' and was enormously influential in European alchemy and esoteric philosophy. It is distinct from Doreal's twentieth-century *Emerald Tablets of Thoth the Atlantean*, with which it is frequently confused.

An American spiritual movement emerging in the late nineteenth century that holds mind and belief to be causally prior to material circumstance — a precursor to the modern 'law of attraction.' It influenced figures from Mary Baker Eddy to Napoleon Hill and persists in contemporary wellness and manifestation culture.

books.title: The Emerald Tablets of Thoth the Atlantean
books.author: Maurice Doreal
books.summary: A 1930s esoteric text in which author Maurice Doreal claims to translate tablets authored by Thoth, a priest-king of lost Atlantis. Written in archaic verse, it presents a cosmology of mental creation, karma, and spiritual law. It is widely circulated in New Age communities, often marketed as ancient, though its modern authorship is documented.

books.title: The Kybalion
books.author: Three Initiates
books.summary: Published in 1908 and attributed pseudonymously to 'Three Initiates,' this book systematizes Hermetic philosophy into seven principles, including the law of cause and effect ('every cause has its effect; every effect has its cause'). Like Doreal's work, it presents itself as recovered ancient teaching. It is a key document of early twentieth-century American Hermeticism and a clear thematic predecessor to the Doreal tablets.

article.fact_check: The post implicitly frames the quote as ancient wisdom. In fact, *The Emerald Tablets of Thoth the Atlantean* is a twentieth-century composition by Maurice Doreal, written in the 1930s. It is not the same as the genuine historical Hermetic text known as the Emerald Tablet (Tabula Smaragdina), which dates to medieval Arabic manuscript tradition. Presenting Doreal's work as recovered ancient scripture is a common framing in New Age circles but is historically inaccurate.
